nameStory: This plant gets its "wild comfrey" name because its leaves resemble those of true comfrey, a European herb historically used for healing. The "southern" part of its name distinguishes it from its northern cousin, though both species can overlap in New England. It's also called "blue houndstongue" because its small blue flowers and rough, tongue-shaped leaves reminded early botanists of a dog's tongue.
description: Southern wild comfrey is a modest woodland wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with a somewhat sprawling habit. It produces small, delicate blue flowers arranged in curving clusters that unfurl like a scorpion's tail - a signature feature of the borage family. The plant has broad, soft leaves that feel distinctly fuzzy to the touch, and it tends to blend quietly into the forest understory rather than making a bold display.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny blue flowers (about 1/4 inch across) arranged in curved, one-sided clusters that gradually unfurl as they bloom, creating a distinctive scorpion-tail shape

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, oval leaves that feel noticeably soft and fuzzy, almost velvety, with prominent veins and a somewhat wrinkled texture

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Loosely branching plant that leans and sprawls rather than standing rigidly upright, often weaving through other woodland plants

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, hard nutlets covered with hooked bristles that stick to clothing and fur - nature's velcro for seed dispersal

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves alternate along the stem (not opposite each other) and gradually get smaller toward the top of the plant

habitat: Southern wild comfrey prefers rich, moist woodland soils in deciduous or mixed forests throughout New England. Look for it in partially shaded areas along woodland edges, in clearings, or where the forest canopy is broken enough to let in dappled sunlight. It often grows alongside other woodland wildflowers and seems to favor spots with good organic matter in the soil.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge as soft, fuzzy rosettes close to the ground before the plant begins its upward growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time when the characteristic blue flower clusters are most visible and the plant reaches full size.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the bristly seed clusters become prominent, while leaves may turn yellowish before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back completely to underground roots, leaving no visible trace above ground until spring.

funFact: This plant was recently given a botanical makeover! Until 2015, it was classified in the genus Cynoglossum, but DNA studies revealed it was different enough to deserve its own genus, Andersonglossum, named after botanist Loran Anderson who studied these plants extensively.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with true forget-me-nots, which also have small blue flowers, but forget-me-nots have much smaller, smoother leaves and grow in wetter areas. Remember: if the leaves feel fuzzy and large, and you're in dry woods rather than near water, you're probably looking at wild comfrey.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, wild comfrey is not closely related to true comfrey (Symphytum species) and shouldn't be used medicinally like its European namesake. The name similarity is purely based on leaf appearance and has caused confusion among foragers and herbalists.
compareHints: Southern wild comfrey differs from its close relative northern wild comfrey mainly in its preferred habitat - southern wild comfrey likes richer, more deciduous forests while northern wild comfrey prefers cooler, more coniferous areas. The flowers and overall appearance are quite similar, making habitat your best clue for identification. Both have the same fuzzy leaves and scorpion-tail flower clusters that distinguish them from other borage family members.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern wild comfrey differs from its close relative wild comfrey (Virginia wild comfrey) mainly by habitat and range—northern wild comfrey prefers cooler boreal forests while Virginia wild comfrey grows in warmer deciduous woods.
